arXiv:1805.01189v1 [math.AP] 03 May 2018

On the existence time for the Kirchhoff equation with periodic boundary conditions

Pietro Baldi    Emanuele Haus

Abstract. We consider the Cauchy problem for the Kirchhoff equation on 𝕋d{\mathbb{T}}^{d} with initial data of small amplitude ε\varepsilon in Sobolev class. We prove a lower bound ε−4\varepsilon^{-4} for the existence time, which improves the bound ε−2\varepsilon^{-2} given by the standard local theory. The proof relies on a normal form transformation, preceded by a nonlinear transformation that diagonalizes the operator at the highest order, which is needed because of the quasilinear nature of the equation.

Keywords. Kirchhoff equation, quasilinear wave equations, Cauchy problems, normal forms, quasilinear normal forms.

MSC2010: 35L72, 35L15, 35Q74, 37J40, 70K45.

Contents. 1 Introduction — 2 Linear transformations — 3 Diagonalization of the order one — 4 Normal form transformation — 5 Proof of Theorem 1.1.

1 Introduction

This paper deals with an old open problem, concerning the global wellposedness of the Kirchhoff equation

∂t​tu−(1+∫Ω|∇u|2​𝑑x)​Δ​u=0\partial_{tt}u-\Big(1+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\,dx\Big)\Delta u=0 (1.1)

with periodic boundary conditions Ω=𝕋d\Omega={\mathbb{T}}^{d} or Dirichlet boundary conditions u|∂Ω=0u|_{\partial\Omega}=0 on a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. In 1940 Bernstein [13] proved that, in the 1-dimensional case Ω=[0,π]\Omega=[0,\pi] with zero boundary conditions u⁡(t,0)=u⁡(t,π)=0u(t,0)=u(t,\pi)=0, the Cauchy problem for (1.1) with initial data

u⁡(0,x)=α⁡(x),∂tu⁡(0,x)=β⁡(x)u(0,x)=\alpha(x),\quad\partial_{t}u(0,x)=\beta(x) (1.2)

is globally wellposed for (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) analytic, and locally wellposed for (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) in the Sobolev space H2×H1H^{2}\times H^{1}. Later on, these results have been extended to higher dimension, also including the periodic setting Ω=𝕋d\Omega={\mathbb{T}}^{d}, proving global wellposedness in larger spaces containing the analytic functions, and local wellposedness in the Sobolev space H32×H12H^{\frac{3}{2}}\times H^{\frac{1}{2}}, with existence time T∼(‖α‖32+‖β‖12)−2T\sim(\|\alpha\|_{\frac{3}{2}}+\|\beta\|_{\frac{1}{2}})^{-2}, see Section 1.3 for a short overview. Nonetheless, the basic question about the existence time for the Cauchy problem with C∞C^{\infty} data, even of small amplitude, is still open. In particular, it is still not known whether the maximal existence time is finite or infinite (notice that the quasilinear wave equation ut​t−(1+ux2)​ux​x=0u_{tt}-(1+u_{x}^{2})u_{xx}=0 on the circle 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}, which looks like (1.3) in one dimension without the integral sign, has a finite blowup time T∼(‖α‖C2+‖β‖C1)−2T\sim(\|\alpha\|_{C^{2}}+\|\beta\|_{C^{1}})^{-2}, as proved by Klainerman and Majda [36]).

In this paper we prove that in the periodic setting Ω=𝕋d\Omega={\mathbb{T}}^{d}, d≥1d\geq 1, for small amplitude initial data (α,β)∈H32×H12(\alpha,\beta)\in H^{\frac{3}{2}}\times H^{\frac{1}{2}} if d=1d=1, or (α,β)∈H2×H1(\alpha,\beta)\in H^{2}\times H^{1} if d≥2d\geq 2, the existence time is at least T∼(‖α‖+‖β‖)−4T\sim(\|\alpha\|+\|\beta\|)^{-4} (Theorem 1.1), which is longer than the time (‖α‖+‖β‖)−2(\|\alpha\|+\|\beta\|)^{-2} provided by the classical local theory. The same result also holds in the case of zero Dirichlet boundary conditions on the cube Ω=[0,π]d\Omega=[0,\pi]^{d} (Remark 1.4). To give a precise statement of our main result, we first introduce some notation.

On the torus 𝕋d{\mathbb{T}}^{d}, it is not restrictive to set the problem in the space of functions with zero average in space, for the following reason. Given initial data α⁡(x),β⁡(x)\alpha(x),\beta(x), we split both them and the unknown u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) into the sum of a zero-mean function and the average term,

α⁡(x)=α0+α~​(x),β⁡(x)=β0+β~​(x),u⁡(t,x)=u0​(t)+u~​(t,x),\alpha(x)=\alpha_{0}+\tilde{\alpha}(x),\quad\beta(x)=\beta_{0}+\tilde{\beta}(x),\quad u(t,x)=u_{0}(t)+\tilde{u}(t,x),

where

∫𝕋dα~(x)dx=0,∫𝕋dβ~(x)dx=0,∫𝕋du~(t,x)dx=0∀t.\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}\tilde{\alpha}(x)\,dx=0,\quad\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}\tilde{\beta}(x)\,dx=0,\quad\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}\tilde{u}(t,x)\,dx=0\quad\forall t.

Then the Cauchy problem

∂t​tu−(1+∫𝕋d|∇u|2​𝑑x)​Δ​u=0,u⁡(0,x)=α⁡(x),∂tu⁡(0,x)=β⁡(x)\partial_{tt}u-\Big(1+\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}|\nabla u|^{2}\,dx\Big)\Delta u=0,\quad u(0,x)=\alpha(x),\quad\partial_{t}u(0,x)=\beta(x) (1.3)

splits into two distinct, uncoupled Cauchy problems: one is the problem for the average u0​(t)u_{0}(t), which is

u0′′​(t)=0,u0​(0)=α0,u0′​(0)=β0u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(t)=0,\quad u_{0}(0)=\alpha_{0},\quad u_{0}^{\prime}(0)=\beta_{0}

and has the unique solution u0​(t)=α0+β0​tu_{0}(t)=\alpha_{0}+\beta_{0}t; the other one is the problem for the zero-mean component u~​(t,x)\tilde{u}(t,x), which is

∂t​tu~−(1+∫𝕋d|∇u~|2​𝑑x)​Δ​u~=0,u~​(0,x)=α~​(x),∂tu~​(0,x)=β~​(x).\partial_{tt}\tilde{u}-\Big(1+\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}|\nabla\tilde{u}|^{2}\,dx\Big)\Delta\tilde{u}=0,\quad\tilde{u}(0,x)=\tilde{\alpha}(x),\quad\partial_{t}\tilde{u}(0,x)=\tilde{\beta}(x).

Thus one has to study the Cauchy problem for the zero-mean unknown u~​(t,x)\tilde{u}(t,x) with zero-mean initial data α~​(x),β~​(x)\tilde{\alpha}(x),\tilde{\beta}(x); this means to study (1.3) in the class of functions with zero average in xx.

For any real s≥0s\geq 0, we consider the Sobolev space of zero-mean functions

H0s​(𝕋d,ℂ)\displaystyle H^{s}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{C}}) :={u(x)=∑j∈ℤd∖{0}ujei​j⋅x:uj∈ℂ,∥u∥s<∞},\displaystyle:=\Big\{u(x)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}\setminus\{0\}}u_{j}e^{ij\cdot x}:u_{j}\in{\mathbb{C}},\ \|u\|_{s}<\infty\Big\}, (1.4)
‖u‖s2\displaystyle\|u\|_{s}^{2} :=∑j∈ℤd∖{0}|uj|2​|j|2​s,\displaystyle:=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}\setminus\{0\}}|u_{j}|^{2}|j|^{2s},

of real-valued functions. For s=0s=0, we write L02L^{2}_{0} instead of H00H^{0}_{0} the space of square-integrable functions with zero average.

The main result of the paper is the following theorem.

Remark 1.2 (Evolution of higher norms).

The constant CC in (1.6) does not depend on ss. This unusual property is a consequence of the special structure of the Kirchhoff equation: if uu is a solution of (1.1), then uu also solves the linear wave equation with time-dependent coefficient ∂t​tu−a⁡(t)​Δ​u=0\partial_{tt}u-a(t)\Delta u=0, with a⁡(t)=1+∫Ω|∇u|2​𝑑xa(t)=1+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\,dx, and therefore v:=|Dx|s​uv:=|D_{x}|^{s}u also solves ∂t​tv−a⁡(t)​Δ​v=0\partial_{tt}v-a(t)\Delta v=0. ∎

Remark 1.3 (Why m0m_{0} in (1.5) is different in dimension d=1d=1 and d≥2d\geq 2).

The proof of Theorem 1.1 is based on a normal form transformation. In the construction of such a normal form, one encounters the differences of the linear eigenvalues |j||j|, j∈ℤdj\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}, as denominators of the transformation coefficients (see (4.12)-(4.13)). On the 1-dimensional torus 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}, the difference ||j|−|k||||j|-|k|| is either zero or ≥1\geq 1, while on 𝕋d{\mathbb{T}}^{d}, d≥2d\geq 2, the differences ||j|−|k||=|j12+…+jd2−k12+…+kd2|||j|-|k||=|\sqrt{j_{1}^{2}+\ldots+j_{d}^{2}}-\sqrt{k_{1}^{2}+\ldots+k_{d}^{2}}| accumulate to zero, with lower bounds ||j|−|k||≥1|j|+|k|||j|-|k||\geq\frac{1}{|j|+|k|}. This is the reason for the different regularity threshold we obtain in dimension 1 or higher. ∎

U:[−π,π]d→ℝ,U(x):=sign(x1x2⋯xd)u(|x1|,…,|xd|)U:[-\pi,\pi]^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}},\quad U(x):=\mathrm{sign}(x_{1}x_{2}\cdots x_{d})u(|x_{1}|,\ldots,|x_{d}|)

A function uu belongs to Hs​(Ω)H^{s}(\Omega), s=1s=1 or s=2s=2 (i.e. the weak partial derivatives of order ≤s\leq s belong to L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega)) with Dirichlet boundary condition u=0u=0 on the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega if and only if (see, e.g., [26], [3]) uu belongs to the domain Vs​(Ω)V_{s}(\Omega) of the fractional Laplacian (−Δ)s/2(-\Delta)^{s/2} on Ω\Omega with zero Dirichlet boundary conditions (a spectrally defined Sobolev space). In such a case, the extension ue​x​tu_{ext} belongs to the Sobolev space H0s​(𝕋d)H^{s}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d}) defined in (1.4). Hence, for initial data α∈H2​(Ω)\alpha\in H^{2}(\Omega), β∈H1​(Ω)\beta\in H^{1}(\Omega) with α=β=0\alpha=\beta=0 on ∂Ω\partial\Omega, one consider the periodic odd extensions αe​x​t∈H02​(𝕋d)\alpha_{ext}\in H^{2}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d}), βe​x​t∈H01​(𝕋d)\beta_{ext}\in H^{1}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d}), and Theorem 1.1 applies.

In dimension d=1d=1, Theorem 1.1 requires less regularity, and it is sufficient that α∈V32​(0,π)\alpha\in V_{\frac{3}{2}}(0,\pi) and β∈V12​(0,π)\beta\in V_{\frac{1}{2}}(0,\pi). One has α∈V32​(0,π)\alpha\in V_{\frac{3}{2}}(0,\pi) if and only if α\alpha belongs to the fractional Sobolev space H32​(0,π)H^{\frac{3}{2}}(0,\pi) on the interval, with α⁡(0)=α⁡(π)=0\alpha(0)=\alpha(\pi)=0, while β∈V12​(0,π)\beta\in V_{\frac{1}{2}}(0,\pi) if and only if β∈H12​(0,π)\beta\in H^{\frac{1}{2}}(0,\pi) with ∫0π|β⁡(x)|2x⁡(π−x)​𝑑x<∞\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{|\beta(x)|^{2}}{x(\pi-x)}\,dx<\infty (see [26], [3]). ∎

1.1 Strategy of the proof

Since the problem is set on the torus 𝕋d{\mathbb{T}}^{d}, which is a compact manifold, no dispersive estimates are available to study the long-time dynamics, and the main point is the analysis of the resonances, for which the key tool is the normal form theory.

The main difficulty in the application of the normal form theory to the Kirchhoff equation is due to the fact that it is a quasilinear PDE. Let us explain this point in more detail. The Kirchhoff equation has the Hamiltonian structure

{∂tu=∇vH​(u,v)=v,∂tv=−∇uH​(u,v)=(1+∫𝕋d|∇u|2​dx)​Δ​u,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\nabla_{v}H(u,v)=v,\\ \partial_{t}v=-\nabla_{u}H(u,v)=\Big(1+\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}|\nabla u|^{2}dx\Big)\Delta u,\end{cases} (1.7)

where the Hamiltonian is

H⁡(u,v)=12​∫𝕋dv2​𝑑x+12​∫𝕋d|∇u|2​𝑑x+(12​∫𝕋d|∇u|2​𝑑x)2,H(u,v)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}v^{2}dx+\frac{1}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}|\nabla u|^{2}dx+\Big(\frac{1}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}|\nabla u|^{2}dx\Big)^{2}, (1.8)

and ∇uH\nabla_{u}H, ∇vH\nabla_{v}H are the gradients with respect to the real scalar product

⟨f,g⟩:=∫𝕋df⁡(x)​g​(x)​𝑑x∀f,g∈L2​(𝕋d,ℝ),\langle f,g\rangle:=\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}f(x)g(x)\,dx\quad\forall f,g\in L^{2}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}}), (1.9)

namely H′​(u,v)​[f,g]=⟨∇uH​(u,v),f⟩+⟨∇vH​(u,v),g⟩H^{\prime}(u,v)[f,g]=\langle\nabla_{u}H(u,v),f\rangle+\langle\nabla_{v}H(u,v),g\rangle for all u,v,f,gu,v,f,g. As a consequence, the first natural attempt is trying to construct the Birkhoff normal form, using close-to-identity, symplectic transformations that are the time one flow of auxiliary Hamiltonians, with the goal of removing the nonresonant terms from the Hamiltonian (1.8), proceeding step by step with respect to the homogeneity orders. When one calculates (at least formally) the first step of this procedure, one finds a transformation Φ\Phi that is bounded on a ball of Hs​(𝕋d,ℝ)×Hs−1​(𝕋d,ℝ)H^{s}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}})\times H^{s-1}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}}) around the origin, but it is not close to the identity as a bounded operator, in the sense that ‖Φ⁡(u,v)−(u,v)‖Hs×Hs−1\|\Phi(u,v)-(u,v)\|_{H^{s}\times H^{s-1}} is not ≲‖(u,v)‖Hs×Hs−13\lesssim\|(u,v)\|_{H^{s}\times H^{s-1}}^{3}, as one needs for the application of the Birkhoff normal form method. Hence the transformed Hamiltonian H⁡(Φ⁡(u,v))H(\Phi(u,v)) cannot be Taylor expanded in homogeneous orders without paying a loss of derivative, and the Birkhoff normal form procedure fails. This is ultimately a consequence of the quasilinear nature of the Kirchhoff equation. Also, even working with more general close-to-identity transformations of vector fields, not necessarily preserving the Hamiltonian structure, the direct application of the Poincaré normal form procedure encounters the same obstacle.

Thus, one has to look at the equation more carefully, distinguishing some terms that are harmless and some other terms that are responsible for the failure of the normal form construction. To this aim, it is convenient to introduce symmetrized complex coordinates (see Section 2), so that the linear wave operator becomes diagonal, and system (1.7) becomes (see (2.6))

{∂tu=−i​Λ​u−i4​⟨Λ⁡(u+u¯),u+u¯⟩​Λ​(u+u¯),∂tu¯=i​Λ​u¯+i4​⟨Λ⁡(u+u¯),u+u¯⟩​Λ​(u+u¯),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=-i\Lambda u-\frac{i}{4}\langle\Lambda(u+\overline{u}),u+\overline{u}\rangle\Lambda(u+\overline{u}),\\ \partial_{t}\overline{u}=i\Lambda\overline{u}+\frac{i}{4}\langle\Lambda(u+\overline{u}),u+\overline{u}\rangle\Lambda(u+\overline{u}),\end{cases} (1.10)

where u¯\overline{u} is the complex conjugate of uu, Λ:=|Dx|\Lambda:=|D_{x}| is the Fourier multiplier of symbol |ξ||\xi|, and ⟨f,g⟩:=∫𝕋df⁡(x)​g​(x)​𝑑x\langle f,g\rangle:=\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}f(x)g(x)\,dx is the same as in (1.9), even for complex-valued functions f,gf,g. We note that the cubic nonlinearity in (1.10) already has a “paralinear” structure, in the sense that, for all functions u,v,hu,v,h, all s≥0s\geq 0, one has

‖⟨Λ​u,v⟩​Λ​h‖s=|⟨Λ​u,v⟩|​‖h‖s+1≤‖u‖12​‖v‖12​‖h‖s+1.\|\langle\Lambda u,v\rangle\Lambda h\|_{s}=|\langle\Lambda u,v\rangle|\,\|h\|_{s+1}\leq\|u\|_{\frac{1}{2}}\|v\|_{\frac{1}{2}}\|h\|_{s+1}.

Hence (1.10) can be interpreted as a linear system whose operator coefficients depend on (u,u¯)(u,\overline{u}), namely

∂t(uu¯)=(−A⁡(u,u¯)−B⁡(u,u¯)B⁡(u,u¯)A⁡(u,u¯))​(uu¯),\partial_{t}\begin{pmatrix}u\\ \overline{u}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-A(u,\overline{u})&-B(u,\overline{u})\\ B(u,\overline{u})&A(u,\overline{u})\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u\\ \overline{u}\end{pmatrix}, (1.11)

where

B⁡(u,u¯)=i4​⟨Λ⁡(u+u¯),u+u¯⟩​Λ,A⁡(u,u¯)=i​Λ+B⁡(u,u¯).B(u,\overline{u})=\frac{i}{4}\langle\Lambda(u+\overline{u}),u+\overline{u}\rangle\Lambda,\quad A(u,\overline{u})=i\Lambda+B(u,\overline{u}).

Since our goal is the analysis of the existence time of the solutions, we calculate the time derivative ∂t(‖u‖s2)\partial_{t}(\|u\|_{s}^{2}) of the Sobolev norms and observe that the diagonal terms A⁡(u,u¯)A(u,\overline{u}) give a zero contribution, while the off-diagonal terms B⁡(u,u¯)B(u,\overline{u}), which couple uu with u¯\overline{u}, give terms that are ≤2​‖u‖122​‖u‖s+122\leq 2\|u\|_{\frac{1}{2}}^{2}\|u\|_{s+\frac{1}{2}}^{2} only. Thus, on the one hand, this energy estimate has a loss of half a derivative and cannot be used for the existence theory; on the other hand, this observation suggests that A⁡(u,u¯)A(u,\overline{u}) can be left untouched by the normal form transformation.

Hence the next natural attempt is the construction of a “partial” normal form transformation Φ\Phi that eliminates the cubic nonresonant terms only from B⁡(u,u¯)B(u,\overline{u}) and does not modify A⁡(u,u¯)A(u,\overline{u}). Indeed, such a transformation exists, it is bounded, and, unlike the full normal form, is close to the identity as a bounded transformation, namely ‖Φ⁡(u,u¯)−(u,u¯)‖Hs×Hs≲‖(u,u¯)‖Hs×Hs3\|\Phi(u,\overline{u})-(u,\overline{u})\|_{H^{s}\times H^{s}}\lesssim\|(u,\overline{u})\|_{H^{s}\times H^{s}}^{3}. Moreover, the cubic resonant terms of B⁡(u,u¯)B(u,\overline{u}) that remain in the transformed system give zero contribution to the energy estimate. However, the transformed system contains unbounded off-diagonal terms of quintic and higher homogeneity order, which produce in the energy estimate the same loss of half a derivative as above.

At this point it becomes clear that one has to eliminate the off-diagonal unbounded terms before the normal form construction. This is at the base of the method developed by Delort in [21], [22] to construct a normal form for quasilinear Klein-Gordon equations on the circle. Roughly speaking, such a method consists in paralinearizing the equation, diagonalizing its principal symbol, so that one can obtain quasilinear energy estimates, and then starting with the normal form procedure. Further developments of this approach can be found in Berti and Delort [14] about gravity-capillary water waves equations on 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}.

The off-diagonal unbounded terms of (1.10) are eliminated in Section 3, where we construct a nonlinear bounded transformation Φ(3)\Phi^{(3)} that conjugates system (1.10) to a new system (see (3.13)) of the form

{∂tu=−i​1+2​P​(u,u¯)​Λ​u+i4​(1+2​P​(u,u¯))​(⟨Λ​u¯,Λ​u¯⟩−⟨Λ​u,Λ​u⟩)​u¯,∂tu¯=i​1+2​P​(u,u¯)​Λ​u¯+i4​(1+2​P​(u,u¯))​(⟨Λ​u¯,Λ​u¯⟩−⟨Λ​u,Λ​u⟩)​u,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=-i\sqrt{1+2P(u,\overline{u})}\,\Lambda u+\dfrac{i}{4(1+2P(u,\overline{u}))}\Big(\langle\Lambda\overline{u},\Lambda\overline{u}\rangle-\langle\Lambda u,\Lambda u\rangle\Big)\overline{u},\\ \partial_{t}\overline{u}=i\sqrt{1+2P(u,\overline{u})}\,\Lambda\overline{u}+\dfrac{i}{4(1+2P(u,\overline{u}))}\Big(\langle\Lambda\overline{u},\Lambda\overline{u}\rangle-\langle\Lambda u,\Lambda u\rangle\Big)u,\end{cases} (1.12)

where P⁡(u,u¯)P(u,\overline{u}) is a real, nonnegative function of time only, defined as P⁡(u,u¯)=φ⁡(14​⟨Λ⁡(u+u¯),u+u¯⟩)P(u,\overline{u})=\varphi(\frac{1}{4}\langle\Lambda(u+\overline{u}),u+\overline{u}\rangle), and φ\varphi is the inverse of the real map x↦x​1+2​xx\mapsto x\sqrt{1+2x}, x≥0x\geq 0. System (1.12) still has the structure (1.11), with the improvement that the off-diagonal part B⁡(u,u¯)B(u,\overline{u}) is now a bounded operator, satisfying

‖B⁡(u,u¯)​h‖s≤‖u‖12​‖h‖s\|B(u,\overline{u})h\|_{s}\leq\|u\|_{1}^{2}\|h\|_{s}

for all s≥0s\geq 0, all u,hu,h. Thanks to the special structure of the Kirchhoff equation, and in particular to the lower bound 14​⟨Λ⁡(u+u¯),u+u¯⟩=∫𝕋d(Re⁡(Λ12​u))2​𝑑x≥0\frac{1}{4}\langle\Lambda(u+\overline{u}),u+\overline{u}\rangle=\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}(\mathrm{Re}\,(\Lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}u))^{2}\,dx\geq 0, the transformation Φ(3)\Phi^{(3)} is global, namely it is defined for all u∈H01​(𝕋d,ℂ)u\in H^{1}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{C}}), and not only for small uu. In (1.10) the off-diagonal term is an operator of order one with coefficient ⟨Λ⁡(u+u¯),u+u¯⟩\langle\Lambda(u+\overline{u}),u+\overline{u}\rangle defined for u∈H012​(𝕋d,ℂ)u\in H^{\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{C}}), while, after Φ(3)\Phi^{(3)}, the new off-diagonal term in (1.12) is an operator of order zero where the coefficient (⟨Λ​u¯,Λ​u¯⟩−⟨Λ​u,Λ​u⟩)(\langle\Lambda\overline{u},\Lambda\overline{u}\rangle-\langle\Lambda u,\Lambda u\rangle) is defined for u∈H01​(𝕋d,ℂ)u\in H^{1}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{C}}). Thus the price to pay for removing the unbounded off-diagonal terms is an increase of 12\frac{1}{2} in the regularity threshold for uu (as if we had integrated by parts).

We remark that, reparametrizing the time variable, the coefficient 1+2​P​(u,u¯)\sqrt{1+2P(u,\overline{u})} of the diagonal part in (1.12) could be normalized to 1; however, this is not needed to prove our result, because these coefficients are independent of xx, and therefore the (unbounded) diagonal terms cancel out in the energy estimate.

In Section 4 we perform one step of normal form. It is a “partial” normal form because it does not modify the harmless cubic diagonal terms. The construction involves the differences |j|−|k||j|-|k|, j,k∈ℤdj,k\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}, j≠kj\neq k, as denominators, which accumulate to zero in dimension d≥2d\geq 2. This produces the different regularity thresholds m0m_{0} in Theorem 1.1, see Remark 1.3. The normal form transformation Φ(4)\Phi^{(4)} is a bounded cubic correction of the identity map, and the off-diagonal terms of the transformed system (4.8), (4.41) remain bounded (unlike in the discussion above). The resonant cubic terms that remain after Φ(4)\Phi^{(4)} create a nonlinear interaction between all Fourier coefficients uj​(t)u_{j}(t) with Fourier modes j∈ℤdj\in\mathbb{Z}^{d} on a sphere |j|=|j|= constant, while any two Fourier coefficients uj​(t),uk​(t)u_{j}(t),u_{k}(t) with |j|≠|k||j|\neq|k| are uncoupled at the cubic homogeneity order. This, together with the conservation of the Hamiltonian, implies that there is no growth of Sobolev norms at the cubic homogeneity order. Therefore all the possible nonlinear effects of growth of Sobolev norms come from the terms of quintic and higher homogeneity order. This leads to the improved energy estimate (see (4.47))

∂t(‖u⁡(t)‖s2)≤C​‖u⁡(t)‖m04​‖u⁡(t)‖s2\partial_{t}(\|u(t)\|_{s}^{2})\leq C\|u(t)\|_{m_{0}}^{4}\|u(t)\|_{s}^{2}

for the transformed system, whence we deduce that the lifespan of the solutions of the original Cauchy problem (1.3) is T∼(‖α‖s+12+‖β‖s−12)−4T\sim(\|\alpha\|_{s+\frac{1}{2}}+\|\beta\|_{s-\frac{1}{2}})^{-4}.

Preliminary further calculations suggest that, after performing the next step of normal form to remove the off-diagonal nonresonant quintic terms, some remaining quintic resonant terms could produce a nonlinear interaction between modes |j|≠|k||j|\neq|k|, so that, in principle, a transfer of energy from low to high Fourier modes, and a growth of Sobolev norms (as in [17], [31], [32], [30] for the semilinear Schrödinger equation on 𝕋2{\mathbb{T}}^{2}) cannot be excluded. The analysis of the quintic order is the objective of a further investigation.

As a final comment, we observe that the general strategy developed in [21], [22], [14] and also adopted in the present paper has a strong analogy with the technique developed for KAM theory for quasilinear PDEs in [6], [7], [25], [15], [8]: the first part of these methods uses pseudo-differential or paradifferential calculus to reduce the linearized or paralinearized operator to some more convenient diagonal form up to a sufficiently smoothing remainder, and it is a reduction with respect to the order of differentiation; then the second part uses normal forms or KAM reducibility schemes to reduce the size of the nonconstant remainders in the operator. In short: first reduce in |Dx||D_{x}|, then in ε\varepsilon.

1.2 Reversible Hamiltonian structure and prime integrals

In this section we make some observations about the structure of the Kirchhoff equation. We do not use them directly in the proof of Theorem 1.1, but they could be interesting per se.

As is well-known, the Kirchhoff equation has a Hamiltonian structure, which is (1.7)-(1.8). Also, since the Hamiltonian (1.8) is even in vv, namely H⁡(u,−v)=H⁡(u,v)H(u,-v)=H(u,v), the Hamiltonian vector field X⁡(u,v)=(∇vH​(u,v),−∇uH​(u,v))X(u,v)=(\nabla_{v}H(u,v),-\nabla_{u}H(u,v)) satisfies X∘S+S∘X=0X\circ S+S\circ X=0, where SS is the involution S⁡(u,v)=(u,−v)S(u,v)=(u,-v). Therefore system (1.7) is time-reversible with respect to SS, which simply means that if u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) is a solution of (1.1), then u⁡(−t,x)u(-t,x) is also a solution of the same equation.

Another observation is that the space of functions u⁡(t,x)=u⁡(t,−x)u(t,x)=u(t,-x) that are even in xx is an invariant subspace for the Kirchhoff equation, as well as the space of odd functions u⁡(t,x)=−u⁡(t,−x)u(t,x)=-u(t,-x). The Fourier support is also invariant for the flow: since the Kirchhoff equation for u⁡(t,x)=∑j∈ℤduj​(t)​ei​j⋅xu(t,x)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}}u_{j}(t)e^{ij\cdot x} is the system of equations

uj′′+|j|2​uj​(1+∑k∈ℤd|k|2​|uk|2)=0∀j∈ℤd,u_{j}^{\prime\prime}+|j|^{2}u_{j}\Big(1+\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}}|k|^{2}|u_{k}|^{2}\Big)=0\quad\forall j\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}, (1.13)

if uj​(0)=uj′​(0)=0u_{j}(0)=u_{j}^{\prime}(0)=0 for some jj, then uj​(t)=0u_{j}(t)=0 for all tt. In particular, if the initial data (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) have finite Fourier support, then the solution exists for all times, and a simple application of finite-dimensional KAM theory shows that some of them are quasi-periodic in time.

In addition to the Hamiltonian, the momentum

M=∫𝕋d(∂tu)∇udxM=\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{d}}(\partial_{t}u)\nabla u\,dx

is also a conserved quantity. Even more, because of the special structure of the Kirchhoff equation, the momentum is the sum M=∑j∈ℤdMjM=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}}M_{j} of infinitely many prime integrals MjM_{j}, defined in the following way. If u⁡(t,x)=∑j∈ℤduj​(t)​ei​j⋅xu(t,x)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}}u_{j}(t)e^{ij\cdot x}, then

Mj=12​i​j​(uj​∂tu−j−u−j​∂tuj),j∈ℤd,M_{j}=\frac{1}{2}ij(u_{j}\partial_{t}u_{-j}-u_{-j}\partial_{t}u_{j}),\quad j\in\mathbb{Z}^{d},

and one has

∂tMj=12​i​j​(uj​∂t​tu−j−u−j​∂t​tuj)=0\partial_{t}M_{j}=\frac{1}{2}ij(u_{j}\partial_{tt}u_{-j}-u_{-j}\partial_{tt}u_{j})=0

because each uju_{j} satisfies (1.13). This observation seems to be new. Since M−j=MjM_{-j}=M_{j}, only “a half” of these prime integrals are independent.

The standard linear changes of coordinates of Section 2 preserve both the Hamiltonian and the reversible structure (SS becomes S1​(u,u¯)=(u¯,u)S_{1}(u,\overline{u})=(\overline{u},u) in complex coordinates). The nonlinear transformation of Section 3 is not symplectic, but it preserves the reversible structure, which is also preserved by the normal form of Section 4.

1.3 Related literature and open questions

Equation (1.1) was introduced by Kirchhoff [35] (and, in one dimension, independently rediscovered in [16] and [45]) to model the transversal oscillations of a clamped string or plate, taking into account nonlinear elastic effects. The first results on the Cauchy problem (1.1)-(1.2) are due to Bernstein. In his 1940 pioneering paper [13], he studied the Cauchy problem on an interval, with Dirichlet boundary conditions, and proved global wellposedness for analytic initial data (α,β)(\alpha,\beta), and local wellposedness for (α,β)∈H2×H1(\alpha,\beta)\in H^{2}\times H^{1}.

After that, the research on the Kirchhoff equation has been developed in various directions, with a different kind of results on compact domains (bounded subset Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} with Dirichlet boundary conditions, or periodic boundary conditions Ω=𝕋d\Omega={\mathbb{T}}^{d}) or non compact domains (Ω=ℝd\Omega={\mathbb{R}}^{d} or “exterior domains” Ω=ℝd∖K\Omega={\mathbb{R}}^{d}\setminus K, with K⊂ℝdK\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} compact domain).

For Ω=ℝd\Omega={\mathbb{R}}^{d}, Greenberg and Hu [29] in dimension d=1d=1 and D’Ancona and Spagnolo [20] in higher dimension proved global wellposedness with scattering for small initial data in weighted Sobolev spaces. Further improvements, dealing with spectrally characterized initial data in larger subsets of the Sobolev spaces, and also including the case of exterior domains, have been more recently obtained, for example, by Yamazaki, Matsuyama and Ruzhansky, see [51], [40] and the many references therein. For global solutions that do not scatter see [39]. Still open is the main question whether the solutions with small initial data in the standard (not weighted) Sobolev spaces Hs​(ℝd)×Hs−1​(ℝd)H^{s}({\mathbb{R}}^{d})\times H^{s-1}({\mathbb{R}}^{d}) are globally defined.

Another research direction regards the extension of global wellposedness, on both compact and non compact domains, to non small initial data that are in a larger space than analytic functions: see, for example, Pokhozhaev [47], Arosio and Spagnolo [4], Nishihara [46], Manfrin [38], Ghisi and Gobbino [28], and the references therein. Still open is the question whether the solutions with initial data of arbitrary size and Gevrey regularity (on any domain) are globally defined.

On compact domains, dispersion, scattering and time-decay mechanisms are not available, and there are no results of global existence, nor of finite time blowup, for initial data (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) of Sobolev, or C∞C^{\infty}, or Gevrey regularity. The local wellposedness in the Sobolev class H32×H12H^{\frac{3}{2}}\times H^{\frac{1}{2}} has been proved by Dickey [23], Medeiros and Milla Miranda [42] and Arosio and Panizzi [3], with existence time of order (‖α‖32+‖β‖12)−2(\|\alpha\|_{\frac{3}{2}}+\|\beta\|_{\frac{1}{2}})^{-2}. Beyond the question about the global wellposedness for small data in Sobolev class, another open question concerns the local wellposedness in the energy space H1×L2H^{1}\times L^{2} or in Hs×Hs−1H^{s}\times H^{s-1} for 1<s<321<s<\frac{3}{2}.

For more details, generalizations (degenerate Kirchhoff equations, Kirchhoff systems, forced and/or damped Kirchhoff equations, etc.) and other open questions, we refer to Lions [37] and the surveys of Arosio [2], Spagnolo [49], and Matsuyama and Ruzhansky [41].

We also mention the recent results [5], [43], [44], [18], which prove the existence of time periodic or quasi-periodic solutions of time periodically or quasi-periodically forced Kirchhoff equations on 𝕋d{\mathbb{T}}^{d}, using Nash-Moser and KAM techniques.

Concerning the normal form theory for quasilinear PDEs, we mention the pioneering work of Shatah [48] on quasilinear Klein-Gordon equations on ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, the abstract result of Bambusi [9], the aforementioned papers of Delort [21], [22] on quasilinear Klein-Gordon on 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}, and the recent literature on water waves by Wu [50], Germain, Masmoudi and Shatah [27], Alazard and Delort [1], Ionescu and Pusateri [34], Craig and Sulem [19], Ifrim and Tataru [33], Berti and Delort [14]. Other applications of normal form techniques to get long-time existence for nonlinear PDEs on compact domains can be found in the work of Bambusi, Nekhoroshev, Grébert, Delort and Szeftel, see e.g. [12], [11], [10], and Feola, Giuliani and Pasquali [24].

2 Linear transformations

In this section we make two elementary, standard linear changes of variables to transform system (1.7) into another one (see (2.6)) where the linear part is diagonal, preserving both the real and the Hamiltonian structure of the problem. These standard transformations are the symmetrization of the highest order (section 2.1) and then the diagonalization of the linear terms (section 2.2).

Λ:=|Dx|:H0s→H0s−1,ei​j⋅x↦|j|​ei​j⋅x\Lambda:=|D_{x}|:H^{s}_{0}\to H^{s-1}_{0},\quad e^{ij\cdot x}\mapsto|j|e^{ij\cdot x}

{∂tu=v∂tv=−(1+⟨Λ​u,Λ​u⟩)​Λ2​u,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=v\\ \partial_{t}v=-(1+\langle\Lambda u,\Lambda u\rangle)\Lambda^{2}u,\end{cases} (2.1)

H⁡(u,v)=12​⟨v,v⟩+12​⟨Λ​u,Λ​u⟩+14​⟨Λ​u,Λ​u⟩2.H(u,v)=\frac{1}{2}\langle v,v\rangle+\frac{1}{2}\langle\Lambda u,\Lambda u\rangle+\frac{1}{4}\langle\Lambda u,\Lambda u\rangle^{2}.

(u,v)=Φ(1)​(q,p)=(Λ−12​q,Λ12​p).(u,v)=\Phi^{(1)}(q,p)=(\Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}q,\Lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}p). (2.2)

which is the Hamiltonian system ∂t(q,p)=J∇H(1)(q,p)\partial_{t}(q,p)=J\nabla H^{(1)}(q,p) with Hamiltonian H(1)=H∘Φ(1)H^{(1)}=H\circ\Phi^{(1)}, namely

H(1)​(q,p)=12​⟨Λ12​p,Λ12​p⟩+12​⟨Λ12​q,Λ12​q⟩+14​⟨Λ12​q,Λ12​q⟩2,J:=(0I−I0).H^{(1)}(q,p)=\frac{1}{2}\langle\Lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}p,\Lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}p\rangle+\frac{1}{2}\langle\Lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}q,\Lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}q\rangle+\frac{1}{4}\langle\Lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}q,\Lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}q\rangle^{2},\quad J:=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\ -I&0\end{pmatrix}. Remark 3.2.

It would be tempting to use the transformation

(fg)=11+ρ​(1ρρ1)​(ηψ)\begin{pmatrix}f\\ g\end{pmatrix}=\frac{1}{1+\rho}\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\ \rho&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\eta\\ \psi\end{pmatrix} (3.14)

instead of (3.5), because (3.14) preserves the formula of QQ:

Q⁡(f,g)=14​⟨Λ⁡(f+g),f+g⟩=14​⟨Λ⁡(η+ψ),η+ψ⟩=Q⁡(η,ψ),Q(f,g)=\frac{1}{4}\langle\Lambda(f+g),f+g\rangle=\frac{1}{4}\langle\Lambda(\eta+\psi),\eta+\psi\rangle=Q(\eta,\psi),

avoiding the use of the inverse function φ\varphi. However, using (3.14) would produce a diagonal term of order zero in the transformed system which does not cancel out in the energy estimate (in fact, on the real subspace ψ=η¯\psi=\bar{\eta} such a diagonal term has a real coefficient). The factor (1−ρ2)−12(1-\rho^{2})^{-\frac{1}{2}} in (3.5) is the only (up to constant factors) choice that eliminates those diagonal terms of order zero. This property is related to the symplectic structure of (2.6). ∎

Lemma 5.1.

There exist universal constants δ0∈(0,14)\delta_{0}\in(0,\frac{1}{4}), C0>0C_{0}>0 such that, for all s≥m0s\geq m_{0} (where m0m_{0} is defined in (1.5)), for all pairs of zero mean real functions (u,v)∈H0s+12​(𝕋d,ℝ)×H0s−12​(𝕋d,ℝ)(u,v)\in H^{s+\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}})\times H^{s-\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}}) satisfying

‖u‖m0+12+‖v‖m0−12≤δ0,\|u\|_{m_{0}+\frac{1}{2}}+\|v\|_{m_{0}-\frac{1}{2}}\leq\delta_{0},

Conversely, if w∈H0s​(𝕋d,ℂ)w\in H^{s}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{C}}) satisfies

then (u,v)=Φ⁡(w,w¯)∈H0s+12​(𝕋d,ℝ)×H0s−12​(𝕋d,ℝ)(u,v)=\Phi(w,\overline{w})\in H^{s+\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}})\times H^{s-\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}}) is a pair of zero mean real functions satisfying

‖u‖s+12+‖v‖s−12≤C0​‖w‖s.\|u\|_{s+\frac{1}{2}}+\|v\|_{s-\frac{1}{2}}\leq C_{0}\|w\|_{s}.

As a consequence, in the following corollary we deduce the equivalence of the Kirchhoff equation (1.3) and the transformed system (4.8).

Corollary 5.2.

Let δ0,C0>0\delta_{0},C_{0}>0 be given by Lemma 5.1. Then, for all s≥m0s\geq m_{0}, if u∈C0​([0,T],H0s+12​(𝕋d,ℝ))∩C1​([0,T],H0s−12​(𝕋d,ℝ))u\in C^{0}([0,T],H^{s+\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}}))\cap C^{1}([0,T],H^{s-\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}})) is a solution of equation (1.3) on some time interval [0,T][0,T] with

maxt∈[0,T]⁡(‖u⁡(t)‖m0+12+‖∂tu⁡(t)‖m0−12)≤δ0,\max_{t\in[0,T]}\big(\|u(t)\|_{m_{0}+\frac{1}{2}}+\|\partial_{t}u(t)\|_{m_{0}-\frac{1}{2}}\big)\leq\delta_{0},

then the pair (w,z)=(w,w¯)∈C0([0,T],H0s(𝕋d,c.c.))(w,z)=(w,\overline{w})\in C^{0}([0,T],H^{s}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},c.c.)) defined as (w⁡(t),w¯​(t))=Φ−1​(u⁡(t),∂tu⁡(t))(w(t),\overline{w}(t))=\Phi^{-1}(u(t),\partial_{t}u(t)) is a solution of system (4.8), satisfying

maxt∈[0,T]⁡‖w⁡(t)‖s≤C0​maxt∈[0,T]⁡(‖u⁡(t)‖s+12+‖∂tu⁡(t)‖s−12).\max_{t\in[0,T]}\|w(t)\|_{s}\leq C_{0}\max_{t\in[0,T]}\big(\|u(t)\|_{s+\frac{1}{2}}+\|\partial_{t}u(t)\|_{s-\frac{1}{2}}\big).

Conversely, if (w,w¯)∈C0([0,T],H0s(𝕋d,c.c.))(w,\overline{w})\in C^{0}([0,T],H^{s}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},c.c.)) is a solution of system (4.8) satisfying

maxt∈[0,T]⁡‖w⁡(t)‖m0≤δ0,\max_{t\in[0,T]}\|w(t)\|_{m_{0}}\leq\delta_{0},

then the pair of real functions (u,v)∈C0​([0,T],H0s+12​(𝕋d,ℝ))×C0​([0,T],H0s−12​(𝕋d,ℝ))(u,v)\in C^{0}([0,T],H^{s+\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}}))\times C^{0}([0,T],H^{s-\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}})) defined as (u⁡(t),v⁡(t))=Φ⁡(w⁡(t),w¯​(t))(u(t),v(t))=\Phi(w(t),\overline{w}(t)) satisfies v=∂tuv=\partial_{t}u and u∈C0​([0,T],H0s+12​(𝕋d))∩C1​([0,T],H0s−12​(𝕋d))u\in C^{0}([0,T],H^{s+\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d}))\cap C^{1}([0,T],H^{s-\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d})) is a solution of equation (1.3) satisfying

maxt∈[0,T]⁡(‖u⁡(t)‖s+12+‖∂tu⁡(t)‖s−12)≤C0​maxt∈[0,T]​‖w⁡(t)‖s.\max_{t\in[0,T]}\big(\|u(t)\|_{s+\frac{1}{2}}+\|\partial_{t}u(t)\|_{s-\frac{1}{2}}\big)\leq C_{0}\max_{t\in[0,T]}\|w(t)\|_{s}.

By a repeated use of Lemma 5.1 and Corollary 5.2 we prove Theorem 1.1.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

The classical local existence and uniqueness theory for the Kirchhoff equation (1.3) (see [3]) and Corollary 5.2 imply the local existence and uniqueness for system (4.8), for every initial data (w0,w0¯)(w_{0},\overline{w_{0}}) in the ball ‖w0‖m0≤δ0\|w_{0}\|_{m_{0}}\leq\delta_{0}.

Let (α,β)∈H0m0+12​(𝕋d,ℝ)×H0m0−12​(𝕋d,ℝ)(\alpha,\beta)\in H^{m_{0}+\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}})\times H^{m_{0}-\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}}) with

ε:=‖α‖m0+12+‖β‖m0−12≤ε0:=δ02​C0.\varepsilon:=\|\alpha\|_{m_{0}+\frac{1}{2}}+\|\beta\|_{m_{0}-\frac{1}{2}}\leq\varepsilon_{0}:=\frac{\delta_{0}}{2C_{0}}.

Let (w0,w0¯):=Φ−1​(α,β)(w_{0},\overline{w_{0}}):=\Phi^{-1}(\alpha,\beta). By Lemma 5.1, one has ‖w0‖m0≤C0​ε≤δ02\|w_{0}\|_{m_{0}}\leq C_{0}\varepsilon\leq\frac{\delta_{0}}{2}, and therefore the Cauchy problem for system (4.8) with initial data (w0,w0¯)(w_{0},\overline{w_{0}}) has a (unique) local solution (w​(t),w¯​(t))(w(t),\overline{w}(t)), whose existence time can be extended as long as w⁡(t)w(t) remains in the ball ‖w‖m0≤δ0\|w\|_{m_{0}}\leq\delta_{0}. By Lemma 4.8,

∂t(‖w⁡(t)‖m02)≤C∗​‖w⁡(t)‖m06.\partial_{t}(\|w(t)\|_{m_{0}}^{2})\leq C_{*}\|w(t)\|_{m_{0}}^{6}.

Hence

‖w⁡(t)‖m0≤‖w0‖m0(1−2​C∗​‖w0‖m04​t)14≤2​‖w0‖m0≤δ0\|w(t)\|_{m_{0}}\leq\frac{\|w_{0}\|_{m_{0}}}{(1-2C_{*}\|w_{0}\|_{m_{0}}^{4}t)^{\frac{1}{4}}}\leq 2\|w_{0}\|_{m_{0}}\leq\delta_{0}

for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], with

T:=C1ε4,C1:=1532​C∗​C04.T:=\frac{C_{1}}{\varepsilon^{4}},\qquad C_{1}:=\frac{15}{32C_{*}C_{0}^{4}}.

Then (u,v):=Φ⁡(w,w¯)(u,v):=\Phi(w,\overline{w}) belongs to C0​([0,T],H0m0+12​(𝕋d,ℝ))×C0​([0,T],H0m0−12​(𝕋d,ℝ))C^{0}([0,T],H^{m_{0}+\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}}))\times C^{0}([0,T],H^{m_{0}-\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}})) and solves (1.7), so that u∈C0​([0,T],H0m0+12​(𝕋d,ℝ))∩C1​([0,T],H0m0−12​(𝕋d,ℝ))u\in C^{0}([0,T],H^{m_{0}+\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}}))\cap C^{1}([0,T],H^{m_{0}-\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}})) solves (1.3) with initial data (α,β)(\alpha,\beta), and ‖u⁡(t)‖m0+12+‖∂tu⁡(t)‖m0−12≤2​C02​ε\|u(t)\|_{m_{0}+\frac{1}{2}}+\|\partial_{t}u(t)\|_{m_{0}-\frac{1}{2}}\leq 2C_{0}^{2}\varepsilon for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T].

If, in addition, (α,β)∈H0s+12​(𝕋d,ℝ)×H0s−12​(𝕋d,ℝ)(\alpha,\beta)\in H^{s+\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}})\times H^{s-\frac{1}{2}}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{R}}) for some s≥m0s\geq m_{0}, then w0∈H0s​(𝕋d,ℂ)w_{0}\in H^{s}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{d},{\mathbb{C}}) and, by Lemma 4.8,

|∂t(‖w⁡(t)‖s2)|≤C∗​‖w⁡(t)‖m04​‖w⁡(t)‖s2≤C∗​(2​‖w0‖m0)4​‖w⁡(t)‖s2|\partial_{t}(\|w(t)\|_{s}^{2})|\leq C_{*}\|w(t)\|_{m_{0}}^{4}\|w(t)\|_{s}^{2}\leq C_{*}(2\|w_{0}\|_{m_{0}})^{4}\|w(t)\|_{s}^{2}
